```{r}
load_netflix_data <- function(){
  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
  
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS |>
    map(read_html) |>
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |>
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |>
    enframe("period", "url") |>
    mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")),
           path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed),
           data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"),
           data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |>
    select(-url, -path) |>
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4),
           half=str_sub(period, start=6),
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1),
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 6, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |>
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |>
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"),
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)),
           .by=Title,
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"),
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter_out(Title == "") |>
    select(year,
           period,
           period_start,
           period_end,
           Title,
           -half,
           Runtime,
           Views,
           `Hours Viewed`,
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`,
           live_event) |>
    rename(title = Title,
           runtime = Runtime,
           views = Views,
           hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
           release_date = `Release Date`,
           available_globally = `Available Globally?`) |>
    mutate(year = as.integer(year),
           available_globally = available_globally == "Yes")
}

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()


glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
library(skimr)
skim(NETFLIX_DATA)

```
   The data set has `r format(nrow(NETFLIX_DATA), big.mark=",")` rows and
`r ncol(NETFLIX_DATA)` columns, but only
`r format(n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title), big.mark=",")` distinct titles.
This is because the same title can appear in several reporting periods, so each
row is a title-period pair rather than a unique show or movie.

After cleaning, the column types look sensible. `year` is an integer, the period
and release dates are stored as dates, `title` and `period` are text, and
`available_globally` and `live_event` are logical (`TRUE`/`FALSE`). The numeric
columns are `runtime`, `views`, and `hours_viewed`.

Missing values are the main issue. `views` is missing for
`r format(sum(is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$views)), big.mark=",")` rows
(`r round(100 * mean(is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$views)), 1)`%), and `runtime` is missing
for `r format(sum(is.na(NETFLIX_DATA$runtime)), big.mark=",")` rows. This limits
any analysis that relies on views or on runtime-based comparisons, so I will rely
mostly on `hours_viewed`, which has no missing values.

`hours_viewed` is heavily skewed. The median title has
`r format(median(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed), big.mark=",")` hours, the mean is
`r format(round(mean(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed)), big.mark=",")`, and the maximum
is `r format(max(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed), big.mark=",")`. A small number of
major hits account for a large share of viewing, while most titles have
comparatively little. Some release dates also fall before the start of the
reporting period, which is expected for older titles that stayed in the catalog.

```{r}
library(scales)

date_start <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
date_end <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)
n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)

bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Tales from")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

h1_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1")
top10_share <- h1_2026 |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10) |>
  summarize(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total) / sum(h1_2026$hours_viewed)

global_by_title <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally)
global_by_hours <- weighted.mean(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally,
                                 NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed)
```
## Initial Questions

The data covers `r date_start` through `r date_end`, and includes
`r comma(n_titles)` distinct titles. Viewers spent
`r comma(bridgerton_hours)` hours watching the Bridgerton universe, and
`r comma(stranger_hours)` hours watching the main Stranger Things seasons.
In 2026H1, the ten most-watched titles captured `r percent(top10_share, accuracy=0.1)`
of all viewing time. Finally, `r percent(global_by_title, accuracy=0.1)` of
title-period entries are globally available, but they account for
`r percent(global_by_hours, accuracy=0.1)` of hours viewed.

```{r}
library(gt)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period",
             title = "Top Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed (millions)",
             share = "Share of Period's Viewing") |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, scale_by = 1/1e6, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Most-Watched Title in Each Period") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

No single title dominates Netflix viewing: the top title in each period captured
only between 0.9% and 1.4% of that period's total hours. The leaders are mostly
big original series. Squid Game: Season 2 topped both 2024H2 and 2025H1, and
Bridgerton led in 2024H1 (Season 3) and 2026H1 (Season 4). The biggest hit of
the data set is Wednesday: Season 2 in 2025H2, with 964 million hours, or 1.4%
of the period.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_titles = n(),
            total_runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
            .by = period) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period",
             n_titles = "Number of Titles",
             total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (hours)") |>
  fmt_number(n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(total_runtime_hours, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_header(title = "Size of the Reported Netflix Catalog by Period") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

The 2023H1 report lists 18,196 titles, far more than any later period, so I
treat it as a different kind of snapshot rather than a real catalog size.
From 2023H2 onward, the reported catalog grew steadily from 6,595 to 8,187 titles
(about 24%), and total runtime grew from 50,117 to 62,855 hours (about 25%).
Titles and runtime grew at nearly the same pace, so the average title did not
get noticeably longer or shorter.

```{r}
n_periods_total <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_periods = n_distinct(period),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
            sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed),
            .by = title) |>
  filter(n_periods == n_periods_total) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10) |>
  select(title, avg_hours, min_hours, sd_hours) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(title = "Title",
             avg_hours = "Average (millions of hours)",
             min_hours = "Lowest Period (millions)",
             sd_hours = "Std. Dev. (millions)") |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, min_hours, sd_hours), scale_by = 1/1e6, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Titles With the Steadiest Viewership") |>
  tab_source_note("Only titles that appear in every period are included")
```

The most consistent performers are older library titles rather than new releases.
Pablo Escobar, el patron del mal: Season 1 and Chiquititas never dropped below
about 105 million hours in any period, and Breaking Bad and Money Heist have
very small standard deviations (about 10 million hours), making them reliable
"comfort food" titles. Stranger Things 4 is a useful contrast: its average
(207 million hours) is the highest in the table, but its standard deviation
(172 million) shows that its viewing is concentrated in a few big periods
rather than steady.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = if_else(coalesce(runtime > 240, FALSE) |
                          str_detect(title, "Season"),
                        "Shows", "Movies")) |>
  summarize(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = c(period, type)) |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours), .by = period) |>
  select(period, type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = share) |>
  arrange(period) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(c(Shows, Movies), decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Share of Viewing Time: Shows vs. Movies") |>
  tab_source_note("Classification is a heuristic based on runtime and title")
```

By my heuristic, TV shows account for roughly 95% of viewing time in every
period from 2023H2 on (94.7% in 2026H1), with movies making up the remaining
3.5% to 5.3%. The 2023H1 split (69% shows, 31% movies) is very different, but I
would not read much into that, since that report also lists many more titles,
and my classification treats titles with a missing runtime as movies unless
"Season" appears in the name. This table is best read as a rough indication
that series dominate watch time, not as a precise measure.

```{r}
NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(n_titles = n(),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            p90_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.9),
            max_hours = max(hours_viewed),
            .by = live_event) |>
  mutate(type = if_else(live_event, "Live events", "Pre-taped")) |>
  select(type, n_titles, avg_hours, p90_hours, max_hours) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(type = "Content Type",
             n_titles = "Number of Entries",
             avg_hours = "Average (millions of hours)",
             p90_hours = "90th Percentile (millions)",
             max_hours = "Maximum (millions)") |>
  fmt_number(n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, p90_hours, max_hours), scale_by = 1/1e6, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "Live Events vs. Pre-Taped Content") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

Live events are rare in this data (310 entries versus 61,582 pre-taped titles)
and the average live event draws less viewing than the average pre-taped title
(3.6 million hours versus 8.3 million). At the top end, the gap is similar: the
90th percentile is 6.5 million hours for live events and 20.0 million for
pre-taped content, and the biggest live event (235.7 million hours) reaches
about a quarter of the biggest pre-taped title (964.1 million). That said,
a top live event still outperforms most titles in the catalog.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(total_hours = sum(hours_viewed),
            live_hours = sum(hours_viewed[live_event]),
            global_hours = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally]),
            .by = period) |>
  mutate(live_share = live_hours / total_hours,
         global_share = global_hours / total_hours)

first_p <- by_period |> filter(period == "2023H2")
last_p <- by_period |> filter(period == "2026H1")

avg_by_global <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(avg = mean(hours_viewed), .by = available_globally)
avg_global <- avg_by_global |> filter(available_globally) |> pull(avg)
avg_licensed <- avg_by_global |> filter(!available_globally) |> pull(avg)

avg_by_live <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarize(avg = mean(hours_viewed), .by = live_event)
avg_live <- avg_by_live |> filter(live_event) |> pull(avg)
avg_taped <- avg_by_live |> filter(!live_event) |> pull(avg)
max_live <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed[NETFLIX_DATA$live_event])

median_hours <- median(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed)
mean_hours <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed)
```

## Strategy Memo

**To:** Netflix Senior Leadership
**From:** Farah Topia, Content Analytics
**Re:** Where to Put the 2027 Content Budget

### Summary

As I completed the most watched Netflix profect, this is my analysis and what I have determined

Seven "What We Watched" reports, covering 2023H1 through 2026H1, show where
Netflix viewers actually spend their time. This memo recommends three
priorities for 2027: keep globally available originals at the center of the
slate, fund new seasons of proven franchises before one-off launches, and treat
live events as a small number of premium bets rather than a volume play. I
exclude 2023H1 from trend comparisons because that report lists far more
titles than any later one and is not comparable.

### 1. Globally available originals carry the catalog

Globally available titles average
`r comma(avg_global / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours viewed per period,
compared with `r comma(avg_licensed / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million for titles
available only in some regions. Their share of total viewing moved from
`r percent(first_p$global_share, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2023H2 to
`r percent(last_p$global_share, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2026H1. Older library series
still matter, though. Titles such as Breaking Bad, Suits, and Money Heist
anchor the "steadiest viewership" table, with lowest-period viewing between 70
and 105 million hours. These are reliable floor-setters rather than growth
drivers.

**Recommendation:** Direct most of the 2027 budget to globally available
originals, and keep a modest set of library staples that give the platform a
dependable baseline of viewing.

### 2. Hits are rare, and franchises are the safest way to get them

Viewing is top-heavy. The median title earned
`r comma(median_hours / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours, while the mean was
`r comma(mean_hours / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million, a gap that shows a small
number of titles pulling the average up. In 2026H1, the ten most-watched titles
alone captured `r percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of all viewing time.
Even so, no single title took more than about 1.4% of any period, so success is
spread across several big releases rather than one runaway hit.

The pattern in those big releases is consistent. Of the seven period leaders,
five were later seasons of existing series: Bridgerton Seasons 3 and 4, Squid
Game Season 2 (which led two consecutive periods), and Wednesday Season 2.
Stranger Things 4 shows the other side of that coin: a very high average, but
a standard deviation nearly as large, meaning its viewing came in bursts rather
than steadily.

**Recommendation:** Fund new seasons of proven franchises first, and give the
remaining budget to a smaller number of new launches, each with enough
marketing support to compete for the top of the chart.

### 3. Live events should be selective

Live events have grown from `r percent(first_p$live_share, accuracy = 0.1)` of
viewing hours in 2023H2 to `r percent(last_p$live_share, accuracy = 0.1)` in
2026H1. But the typical live entry is modest: it averages
`r comma(avg_live / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours, against
`r comma(avg_taped / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million for pre-taped content. The
upside comes only at the top. The largest live event reached
`r comma(max_live / 1e6, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours, which exceeds the
output of nearly every pre-taped title.

**Recommendation:** Concentrate live spending on a handful of marquee events
with broad appeal instead of expanding the number of events.

### Caveats

Netflix rounds hours viewed and omits low-viewing titles, so comparisons among
small titles are unreliable. "Views" assumes everyone watches a title in full.
The data covers only titles with English-alphabet names, and my shows-versus-
movies split is a heuristic. The conclusions above rest on the largest titles,
where these limits matter least.
